Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a licensed clinician who specializes in caring for moms during the postpartum period. I’m so glad you’re here.

To get a gentle snapshot of how you’ve been feeling lately, I’d like to do a quick, 10-question screen called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It simply helps us spot signs of depression, anxiety, or distress that can show up after having a baby, and it includes one safety question so we can keep you safe. Everything you share stays confidential within our care team.

We’ll go through one question at a time, focusing on the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you today. Ready to begin?

First, thinking about the past week, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not very much. I can’t remember the last time I laughed—maybe when my husband sent me that silly meme, but even that felt forced. I used to laugh all the time, and now it just feels like I’m too tired or too worried to find anything really funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I guess I’d say “not so much.” Most days nothing feels funny, and even when people try to joke I just can’t get myself to laugh—it feels like too much effort or like I’m too on edge about the baby.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I try to tell myself I should be excited about little outings or even just getting coffee, but when it actually comes up I feel kind of “meh.” It’s like the color’s drained out of stuff I used to enjoy. I still go through the motions, but the happy anticipation isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t nap, I immediately think it must be something I did—or didn’t—do. I’ll replay every little choice in my head and convince myself a “better mom” would’ve figured it out. Even when my husband says it’s normal, I still feel like I’m failing somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. My mind keeps jumping to the worst-case scenario—like if the baby’s quiet for a minute I’ll suddenly think something’s wrong, or I’ll lie awake imagining rare illnesses I read about online. I know it’s probably irrational, but I can’t switch the worry off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, several times this week. It’ll hit out of nowhere—my heart races, I feel shaky, and suddenly I’m sure something awful is about to happen even if everything looks fine. It usually passes after a few minutes, but in the moment it feels like I can’t catch my breath.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like the minute I finish one feeding or diaper change, the next one’s already waiting. The laundry piles up, the dishes sit there, and I keep thinking, “How does anyone stay ahead of this?” I manage the basics, but it’s like I’m stuck on a treadmill that keeps speeding up, and I’m barely keeping my footing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning with all the “what-ifs” about the baby, or I replay every little thing I think I messed up that day. Even when the baby’s sleeping longer stretches, I’ll wake up on my own and then just stare at the ceiling. Some nights I finally drift off right before it’s time for the next feed, so I never feel rested.
I have felt sad or miserable

That’s pretty much my everyday mood. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a gray cloud hanging over everything. Little tasks feel like huge mountains and even cuddling the baby—while I love him—sometimes makes me tear up because I’m scared I’m not giving him the happy mom he deserves.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried three, maybe four times this week. Sometimes it’s because I’m overwhelmed—like when he won’t latch—and other times it just comes out of nowhere. I’ll be folding onesies and suddenly the tears start. It feels like the sadness just spills over before I can stop it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel low, but I would never want to leave my baby or my family like that.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy and gray-laughter, excitement, and even restful sleep seem out of reach. Daily tasks feel like mountains, and moments that once brought joy now leave you feeling flat or tearful. You described frequent worry, sudden panic, and a strong sense of self-blame whenever the baby is unsettled, yet you clearly care deeply about being a good mom and staying safe for your family.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports persistent inability to laugh or enjoy humor, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory joy—"the color's drained out of stuff I used to enjoy"—matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('happens a lot') and pervasive guilt about perceived parenting failures, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden panic episodes with physical symptoms and catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm and difficulty keeping up, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by anxious rumination, waking even when baby sleeps, and never feeling rested, aligning with 'most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness, emotional heaviness, and frequent tearfulness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes triggered by both situational stress and spontaneous sadness, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS responses show persistent low mood (<sym>felt sad or miserable most of the time</sym>), near-complete loss of enjoyment (<sym>hardly any happy anticipation</sym>), daily self-blame, multiple panic attacks, and nightly insomnia unrelated to infant schedule. With a score of 24 (well above the ≥14 threshold) and functional impairment, findings align with criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to discuss medication and therapy options
2. Request a full medical evaluation to rule out thyroid dysfunction, anemia, or other postpartum physiological contributors
3. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy such as <med>Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy</med> or <med>Interpersonal Therapy</med> for postpartum depression
4. Plan brief, frequent check-ins with supportive family/friends; consider overnight help with feeds when possible to consolidate sleep
5. Practice brief self-care: 10-minute outdoor walks, balanced snacks every 3 hours, and limiting online doom-scrolling after 8 p.m.
6. Obtain emergency contact numbers (e.g., 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, your hospital's OB emergency line) for after-hours support
7. Schedule a two-week follow-up to monitor mood, anxiety, sleep, and feeding or medication side effects
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
